title: Why 'the right cheek'?
summary: A right-handed blow to someone's right cheek is a backhand, and the Mishnah fines a backhanded slap double. Walter Wink reads Jesus' words from there: turning the other cheek offers only the left, which can be struck only as an equal. Augustine read the saying as a readiness of the heart.
body: Matthew specifies the right cheek. For a right-handed striker to hit the right cheek, the blow is a backhand. The Mishnah prices the difference: a slap costs 200 zuz (dinars) in damages, a slap with the back of the hand 400, in a list of payments for humiliation. Wink reads the backhand as an insult rather than a fight, the way a master struck a slave.

On Wink's reading, turning the other cheek is neither retaliation nor submission. Offering the left cheek makes a second backhand impossible; the striker must either stop or hit with an open hand or fist, the way one strikes an equal, and the gesture takes the humiliation out of the blow.

Augustine read the saying as about 'the preparation of the heart, not the outward act': a readiness to absorb injury without vengeance, with nothing made of the 'right'. The Mishnah's fine is evidence; Wink's tactic and Augustine's disposition are interpretations.

title: The second mile and the right of requisition
summary: 'Compel' is angareuō, the technical word for a soldier's legal right to requisition a civilian's labour or animal. The same word is used when the soldiers press Simon of Cyrene to carry the cross.
body: The Persian empire ran a relay post (angareion) whose couriers could commandeer horses and men; the word passed into Greek and Latin and by Roman times meant any official requisition of transport or labour. Matthew uses it here and again in 27:32, where Simon of Cyrene is 'compelled' to carry Jesus' cross — the one act of angareia the Gospels narrate.

An inscription found at Sagalassos in Pisidia (modern Turkey) preserves an edict of the governor Sextus Sotidius Strabo Libuscidianus, issued under Tiberius, setting out exactly what soldiers and officials could demand of the locals: so many carts and mules, at fixed rates, for so far — and complaining that they abused the right. The edict is contemporary with Jesus, and shows the practice both regulated by law and complained of by the governor as abused.

The distance is a Roman mile (milion, about 1,480 m). Walter Wink reads the second mile as turning coercion into a free act, leaving the soldier, who on his account could be punished for exceeding his allowance, in the debtor's position. That is Wink's reading, as on the 'right cheek' card; the text says only 'go with him two miles'.

title: Tunic, cloak, and the law that protected the poor
summary: Torah required a creditor who took a poor man's cloak as a pledge to return it by sunset, because it was what he slept in. In Matthew, Jesus tells the one sued for his tunic to give up his cloak as well.
body: A first-century Judean man typically owned two garments: the chitōn (tunic, worn next to the skin) and the himation (cloak, the heavy outer wrap). Exodus 22:26–27 and Deuteronomy 24:12–13 require a lender who takes a cloak as collateral to return it by sunset: 'his cloak is the only covering he has for his body. What else will he sleep in?' The laws say nothing of the tunic.

Matthew's version has the opponent suing for the tunic, and Jesus telling the one sued to let him have the cloak as well, the garment the pledge laws protect overnight. In Luke the order is reversed, and there is no lawsuit: 'if someone takes your cloak, do not withhold your tunic as well' (6:29).
An ostracon from Mesad Hashavyahu (7th century BC) records a field labourer's petition to a governor complaining that an official had seized his garment and asking for it back.

title: Betrothed, yet needing a divorce
summary: Joseph is 'pledged' to Mary but plans to 'divorce' her. Jewish betrothal (erusin) was legally marriage: the couple did not yet live together, but ending it required a bill of divorce, and unfaithfulness counted as adultery.
body: Marriage came in two stages roughly a year apart. At betrothal the man paid the bride-price and the woman was legally his wife; at the wedding (nissuin) she moved into his house. Deuteronomy 22:23–24 already treats a betrothed woman as a 'wife' and her seducer as an adulterer, and the Mishnah's tractate on betrothal (Kiddushin 1:1) opens with the three ways a woman is 'acquired' as a wife — money, a document, or intercourse.

Matthew calls Joseph Mary's 'husband' (1:19) while saying they had not yet 'come together' (1:18), and has Joseph, 'a righteous man … unwilling to disgrace her publicly', resolve 'to divorce her quietly'.

title: Reclining at table — why her hair could reach his feet
summary: At a formal meal guests lay on couches on their left side, feet pointing away from the table. A guest's feet lay behind him: in Luke 7 a woman anoints Jesus' feet from behind, and in John 13 the disciple whom Jesus loved leans back against Him.
body: The Gospels' dinner scenes use the verbs for 'recline' (anakeimai, katakeimai), not 'sit'. Diners lay on couches (the Greek triklinion, 'three couches', gives us the room's name) arranged around a low table, propped on the left elbow, heads toward the table and feet stretched out behind.

The Gospels' details agree with that arrangement: the woman in Luke 7 stands 'behind him at his feet'; Mary in John 12 anoints his feet and wipes them with her hair; in Mark 14 the flask is poured on his head as he reclines; and in John 13 the beloved disciple can lean back on Jesus' chest to whisper a question. Dining rooms of this type have been excavated in Herodian palaces and in the wealthy houses of Jerusalem's Herodian Quarter.

title: 'No room in the inn' — or in the guest room?
summary: Luke's word in 2:7 is kataluma, which he uses again for the upper 'guest room' of the Last Supper. When he means a commercial inn (Luke 10:34) he uses a different word, pandocheion.
body: The picture of an innkeeper turning the couple away rests on the translation 'inn', which the BSB keeps. Luke knows the ordinary word for a paid inn — pandocheion, the place the Good Samaritan pays two denarii — and does not use it here. Kataluma is a lodging place or guest room; in Luke 22:11 (and Mark 14:14) it is the furnished upper room where Jesus eats the Passover.

Kenneth Bailey reconstructs the village house of the period with a single family room, a raised guest space, and a lower area where animals were brought in at night, with mangers cut into the floor or wall between them. On his reading Joseph and Mary were taken in by relatives in Bethlehem, the guest room was already full, and the baby was laid in the manger at the family end of the house. Luke's choice of words is evidence; Bailey's house is an interpretation.

title: A day begins at sunset
summary: 'There was evening, and there was morning' — the Hebrew day ran from sunset to sunset.
body: Genesis 1 counts each day evening-first, and Leviticus 23:32 makes the rule explicit for the Day of Atonement: 'from evening to evening'. Sabbath therefore began at Friday sunset. Mark sets Jesus' first day in Capernaum on a Sabbath (1:21), and the townspeople bring their sick 'that evening, after sunset' (1:32), when by this reckoning the Sabbath had ended. Luke sets the burial on 'Preparation Day, and the Sabbath was beginning' (23:54).
The same convention explains why Passover 'day' spans what are two calendar dates in the Roman reckoning, and why Jewish holidays today still begin at nightfall.

title: The fringe she touched
summary: The woman with the haemorrhage reaches for 'the fringe of his garment' — the kraspedon, the tasselled corner Numbers 15 commands every Israelite man to wear as a memorial of the commandments.
body: Numbers 15:38-39 tells Israel to make tassels on the corners of their garments, with a cord of blue in each, 'so that you may look at it and remember all the commandments of the LORD'. Deuteronomy 22:12 repeats the instruction. The Hebrew is tzitzit; the Greek translators and the Gospel writers use kraspedon, which English versions render fringe, tassel, hem or border.
Matthew 9:20 says the woman touched 'the fringe of His cloak', the kraspedon. Matthew 14:36 and Mark 6:56 use the same word: the sick in the villages ask to touch just the kraspedon.

Leviticus 15:25-27 places a woman with a chronic flow of blood in a state of ritual impurity that passes to whatever she lies or sits on and to whoever touches it. Hers had lasted twelve years (Mark 5:25), and she came 'through the crowd behind Him' (5:27).
The tassels appear again in Matthew 23:5, where Jesus says of the scribes and Pharisees, 'All their deeds are done for men to see … they lengthen their tassels.'

Woollen tassels and cords of blue have been recovered from the Judean desert caves of the Bar Kokhba period, so the practice is attested physically as well as textually — though those finds are a century after the Gospels.

title: 'I, Tertius, who wrote this letter, greet you'
summary: One of Paul's scribes signs his own name in Romans, and Paul several times writes a closing 'in my own hand'. E. Randolph Richards sets these beside the papyrus letters of the period, dictated to a secretary and signed by the sender.
body: Writing on papyrus with a reed pen was a trained skill, and Richards shows from surviving papyrus letters that senders often dictated to a secretary, an amanuensis: a practised professional hand for the body, then a few lines and a signature added by the sender.

Romans ends with the scribe stepping briefly out of role: 'I, Tertius, who wrote this letter, greet you in the Lord' (Romans 16:22) — a Roman name common among slaves and freedmen. Elsewhere Paul takes the pen himself for the closing: 'the greeting is in my own hand' (1 Corinthians 16:21; Colossians 4:18), 'see with what large letters I am writing to you with my own hand' (Galatians 6:11), and in Philemon 19 an IOU written out personally. 2 Thessalonians 3:17 makes the signature a deliberate authentication: 'this is the sign of genuineness in every letter of mine'.
The same letter warns against a 'letter seeming to be from us' (2 Thessalonians 2:2).

Richards documents a range of secretarial practice, from strict shorthand to near co-authorship, and offers dictation as part of the explanation for shifts of style between letters; how much latitude Paul gave is not recorded. 1 Peter 5:12, 'by Silvanus I have written to you briefly', has been read as naming a secretary; Richards reads the phrase as naming the letter's carrier.

title: A sandal, ten witnesses, and a property deal at the gate
summary: Boaz does not marry Ruth privately. He convenes a court in the town gateway, makes the nearer kinsman decline in public, and takes a sandal as the receipt. Ruth 4 records it as a legal transaction.
body: The gate of a walled town was its courthouse. The gateway of an Iron Age Israelite city was a deep chambered structure with benches built into the side rooms — excavated examples survive at Dan, Gezer and Beersheba — and it was where everyone entering or leaving passed. Deuteronomy 21:19, 22:15 and 25:7 all send disputes 'to the elders at the gate'. Boaz sits down there, stops the man he needs and seats ten elders (Ruth 4:1-2); Robert Hubbard reads this as convening a court.

Two separate laws are in play. Leviticus 25:25 gives a near relative the right and duty to redeem land a poor kinsman has had to sell. Deuteronomy 25:5-10 requires a dead man's brother to marry the widow and raise an heir in his name. Boaz presents the field first; the nearer redeemer accepts. Only then does Boaz add that the field comes with Ruth, and the man withdraws, 'or I would jeopardize my own inheritance' (Ruth 4:6), which Hubbard reads as the risk of the land passing to an heir counted to another man's line.

Then the sandal. Ruth 4:7 explains the custom: 'in former times in Israel, concerning the redemption or exchange of property, to make any matter legally binding a man would remove his sandal and give it to the other party'. It is related to, but not the same as, Deuteronomy 25:9, where the widow herself pulls the sandal off the refusing brother-in-law and spits in his face; that version is a shaming penalty. In Ruth the man takes his own sandal off and hands it over, and nobody spits. The narrator explains it as a custom of 'former times in Israel'.

Boaz is not the nearest kinsman, and the levirate law of Deuteronomy 25 names a brother, not a more distant relative. Hubbard reads his acting beyond both statutes, before witnesses, as the book's theme of hesed, loyal kindness.

title: Water and light at the Feast of Tabernacles
summary: On the last day of Tabernacles Jesus cried, 'If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink', and soon after, 'I am the light of the world'. The Mishnah describes the feast's two great rites in the temple: water drawn from Siloam and poured at the altar, and golden lamps that lit every courtyard in Jerusalem.
body: Mishnah Sukkah 4:9: each morning of the feast a priest filled 'a golden jug with a capacity of three log with water from the Siloam pool', carried it in through the Water Gate to the sound of trumpets, climbed the altar and poured it into a silver basin. A priest who once poured it on his feet instead (a Sadducee, in the William Davidson translation's explanation) was pelted with the people's citrons.

Sukkah 5:2-4: at the end of the first day golden lamps were set up in the Women's Court, on poles with four basins each, lit with wicks of worn priestly garments, 'and the light … was so bright that there was not a courtyard in Jerusalem that was not illuminated'. Men danced with torches through the night while the Levites played on the fifteen steps.

John sets these sayings at the feast: living water offered 'on the last and greatest day' (7:37), 'I am the light of the world' spoken in the temple courts (8:12, 20), and soon after a blind man sent to wash in Siloam (9:7). Zechariah 14, read on the feast's first day, promises living water flowing from Jerusalem (14:8).
The Mishnah was compiled about AD 200, after the temple's fall. It describes the rites as remembered, and how closely they match the practice of Jesus's day cannot be checked.

title: Purim on the 14th or the 15th — and an argument over Esther
summary: Esther fixes Purim on the 14th of Adar, and the 15th for Susa, where the fighting lasted a day longer. The Mishnah keeps the split: walled cities read the scroll on the 15th. The Talmud also records a sage who held that Esther, which never names God, did not 'defile the hands' as Scripture does.
body: Esther 9 explains the two dates: the Jews of the provinces rested on the 14th of Adar, but in Susa they fought on the 13th and 14th and rested on the 15th (9:17-19). Mordecai's letters establish both days (9:21).

The Mishnah turns it into a rule for reading the scroll, the Megillah: 'Cities that have been surrounded by a wall since the days of Joshua, son of Nun, read the Megilla on the fifteenth of Adar, whereas villages and large towns that have not been walled since the days of Joshua … read it on the fourteenth.' Jerusalem still keeps Purim on the 15th.

Esther never mentions God, and the Talmud preserves a dispute over its standing. Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel: 'The book of Esther does not render the hands ritually impure' — the mark of a holy scroll — and resolves the tension with Shmuel's other view that Esther was 'stated with the inspiration of the Divine Spirit' by saying it was given to be read aloud but not written as Scripture. The book was read in the synagogues all the same.
